content: Calcium acetate is a medication classified as a Genitourinary Agent. It is FDA-approved for the treatment of hyperphosphatemia in patients with end-stage renal failure. Common adverse reactions associated with its use include hypercalcemia, nausea, and vomiting. Adult Indications and Dosage Indications: Calcium acetate capsules are indicated for the control of hyperphosphatemia in patients with end-stage renal failure. They do not promote aluminum absorption. Dosage: The recommended initial dose for adult dialysis patients is two capsules with each meal. The dosage may be gradually increased to lower serum phosphate levels below 6 mg/dL, provided hypercalcemia does not develop. Most patients require three to four capsules with each meal. Pediatric Indications and Dosage There is limited information regarding the FDA-labeled or off-label use of calcium acetate in pediatric patients. Contraindications Calcium acetate is contraindicated in patients with hypercalcemia. Warnings Patients with end-stage renal failure may develop hypercalcemia when calcium is administered with meals. No other calcium supplements should be given concurrently with calcium acetate capsules. Progressive hypercalcemia due to calcium acetate overdose can be severe and may require emergency measures. Chronic hypercalcemia can lead to vascular and soft-tissue calcification. Serum calcium levels should be monitored twice weekly during the early dose adjustment period. The calcium-phosphate product (Ca x P) should not exceed 66. Radiographic evaluation of suspected anatomical regions may help in the early detection of soft-tissue calcification. Precautions Excessive calcium acetate dosage can induce hypercalcemia. During the early treatment phase, serum calcium should be determined twice weekly. If hypercalcemia develops, the dosage should be reduced or the treatment discontinued immediately, depending on the severity. Calcium acetate should not be given to patients on digitalis, as hypercalcemia may precipitate cardiac arrhythmias. Therapy should always begin at a low dose and should not be increased without careful monitoring of serum calcium levels. An estimate of daily calcium intake should be made initially, and adjustments should be made as needed. Serum phosphorus should also be determined periodically. Adverse Reactions Clinical Trials Experience: Nausea has occasionally been reported during calcium acetate therapy. Hypercalcemia may occur, which can be asymptomatic or present with symptoms such as constipation, anorexia, nausea, and vomiting. Severe hypercalcemia (Ca > 12 mg/dL) may cause confusion, delirium, stupor, or coma. Mild hypercalcemia can be managed by reducing the dose or temporarily discontinuing therapy. Severe hypercalcemia may require acute hemodialysis and discontinuation of calcium acetate therapy. Reducing dialysate calcium concentration may decrease the incidence and severity of hypercalcemia induced by calcium acetate. The long-term effects of calcium acetate on vascular or soft-tissue calcification progression have not been determined. Isolated cases of pruritus, possibly representing allergic reactions, have been reported. Postmarketing Experience: Limited information is available regarding postmarketing experience with calcium acetate. Drug Interactions There is limited information regarding drug interactions with calcium acetate. Use in Specific Populations Pregnancy: Calcium acetate is classified as Pregnancy Category C by the FDA. Animal reproduction studies have not been conducted, and it is unknown whether calcium acetate can cause fetal harm or affect reproductive capacity. It should only be used during pregnancy if clearly needed. Labor and Delivery: No FDA guidance is available on the use of calcium acetate during labor and delivery. Nursing Mothers: No FDA guidance is available on the use of calcium acetate in nursing mothers. Pediatric Use: Safety and effectiveness in pediatric patients have not been established. Geriatric Use: In clinical studies, 25% of subjects were aged 65 and older, and 7% were aged 75 and older. No overall differences in safety or effectiveness were observed between these subjects and younger subjects. However, greater sensitivity in some older individuals cannot be ruled out. Gender and Race: No specific FDA guidance is available regarding the use of calcium acetate in specific gender or racial populations. Renal and Hepatic Impairment: No specific FDA guidance is available regarding the use of calcium acetate in patients with renal or hepatic impairment. Females of Reproductive Potential and Males: No specific FDA guidance is available regarding the use of calcium acetate in these populations. Immunocompromised Patients: No specific FDA guidance is available regarding the use of calcium acetate in immunocompromised patients. Administration and Monitoring Administration: Calcium acetate is administered orally. Monitoring: Serum calcium levels should be monitored twice weekly during the early dose adjustment period. Therapy should always begin at a low dose and should not be increased without careful monitoring of serum calcium levels. Overdosage Administration of calcium acetate in excess of the appropriate daily dosage can cause severe hypercalcemia. Pharmacology Mechanism of Action: In patients with advanced renal insufficiency (creatinine clearance < 30 mL/min), phosphate retention and hyperphosphatemia occur. Phosphate retention plays a key role in secondary hyperparathyroidism, osteodystrophy, and soft-tissue calcification. Calcium acetate binds dietary phosphate in the intestine, forming insoluble calcium phosphate, which is excreted in the feces. This reduces the fraction of dietary phosphate absorbed. Pharmacokinetics: Calcium acetate is highly soluble at neutral pH, making calcium readily available for binding to phosphate in the proximal small intestine. Orally administered calcium acetate is systemically absorbed up to approximately 40% under fasting conditions and up to 30% under non-fasting conditions. Clinical Studies and Nonclinical Toxicology Limited information is available regarding clinical studies and nonclinical toxicology of calcium acetate. How Supplied Calcium acetate capsules are supplied as white opaque/blue opaque capsules imprinted with 54215 on the cap and body. Patient Counseling Information Limited information is available regarding patient counseling for calcium acetate. Precautions with Alcohol The interaction between alcohol and calcium acetate has not been established. Patients should consult their doctor regarding the effects of alcohol consumption while taking this medication.
